note: Original principles for strategy, influence and judgement. They are inspired by the broad theme of power and strategy studied in history and political science, and are written for three purposes: using influence ethically, recognising manipulation, and deciding well. They are not a copy of any published book; for a specific book, read the original.

power.title: Credibility is the currency
power.principle: A promise carries weight only when it is costly to break or easy to check.
power.defence: Ask what a promise costs the person who made it. If nothing, weigh it lightly.

power.title: Reputation compounds
power.principle: Consistent, honest dealing builds leverage that grows with each round.
power.defence: Check a track record before trusting someone with something important.

power.title: Do not bluff what can be called
power.principle: A bluff works only when the other side cannot cheaply test it.
power.defence: Test a bold claim with a small, low-cost request before committing.

power.title: Make commitments visible
power.principle: Others can rely on you only if they can see what you have committed to.
power.defence: Notice small promises that go unkept. They are early warnings.

power.title: Overcommitment is a trap
power.principle: Investments made to win a contest can lock you into losing it.
power.defence: Set your walk-away point before you start, and write it down.

power.title: Be the same across audiences
power.principle: Consistency across different people builds trust; contradiction spreads quickly.
power.defence: Watch for people who tell each audience a different story.

power.title: Find the information gap
power.principle: Power often sits where one side knows something the other does not.
power.defence: Ask what the other side knows that you do not, and how you could find out.

power.title: Read what is not said
power.principle: Silence can be as informative as any statement, especially when disclosure is expected.
power.defence: Note what a party avoids saying, and ask why.

power.title: Corroborate independently
power.principle: Claims that come from one source, or from sources sharing an origin, are weak evidence.
power.defence: Check important claims with a source that has no stake in the answer.

power.title: Update on evidence, not on drama
power.principle: A vivid story moves belief more than its evidence justifies.
power.defence: Write down your starting view and how strongly each new fact should move it.

power.title: Distrust false dilemmas
power.principle: Presenting only two options hides the ones that matter most.
power.defence: List at least three options before choosing between any two.

power.title: The first explanation is the riskiest
power.principle: The first plausible story tends to stick, even when later evidence contradicts it.
power.defence: Assign someone to argue the opposite before you act.

power.title: Crowds reveal what people expect
power.principle: What others do often reflects what they think others will do, not the underlying facts.
power.defence: Form your own view from your own evidence before looking at the crowd.

power.title: Manufactured urgency shrinks thinking
power.principle: Deadlines are often created to stop careful comparison.
power.defence: When a deadline appears, take a short pause and ask who set it and why.

power.title: Build coalitions before you need them
power.principle: Allies gathered in advance are cheaper and more reliable than allies gathered in a crisis.
power.defence: Notice when others quietly gather allies against you.

power.title: Make the cooperative path visible
power.principle: People cooperate more when they can see that others are cooperating.
power.defence: Publish contributions and results so that cooperation is seen and rewarded.

power.title: Give first, then expect return
power.principle: A small, early act of good faith often starts reciprocity.
power.defence: Distinguish reciprocity from a favour that creates a debt you did not agree to.

power.title: Consensus is built, not announced
power.principle: Decisions stick when the people affected were consulted before the vote.
power.defence: Ask who was consulted before a decision that affects you.

power.title: Limit blank-cheque commitments
power.principle: An unlimited promise to an ally can pull you into conflicts you did not choose.
power.defence: Agree specific, limited commitments with clear consultation rules.

power.title: Notice when you are being divided
power.principle: Opponents are weaker together; offering separate deals to each is a common way to split a group.
power.defence: Compare the terms offered to each member of a group, and share them openly.

power.title: Influence through usefulness
power.principle: Influence that rests on real value lasts longer than pressure or favours.
power.defence: Notice when a favour creates an obligation that was never discussed.

power.title: Loyalty is tested over time
power.principle: Support is kept by reward and by the expectation that others will stay loyal too.
power.defence: Watch who gains from your loyalty, and whether those gains are shared.

power.title: Patience is leverage when the other side pays for delay
power.principle: The party that can afford to wait usually gets the better share.
power.defence: Know who bears the cost of waiting, and whether it is you.

power.title: Move first when it commits the other side
power.principle: A credible first move can shape the choices left to others.
power.defence: Do not rush into irreversible moves before you know what they commit you to.

power.title: Stop before sunk costs decide for you
power.principle: Money or effort already spent should not determine whether to spend more.
power.defence: Ask only what the next unit of effort will buy, not what has been spent.

power.title: Strike at the weakest point
power.principle: A spread-out defence is only as strong as its weakest front.
power.defence: Map your weakest points and reinforce them before they are tested.

power.title: Concentrate where it decides
power.principle: Force or effort concentrated on the decisive point usually beats the same effort spread thin.
power.defence: Identify the one point that decides the outcome, and protect it.

power.title: Wait for the focal signal when many are watching
power.principle: Acting alone is risky; a clear signal lets many people move together.
power.defence: Before acting publicly, check whether others are moving too, using reliable information.

power.title: Set a budget for learning
power.principle: Exploring options gathers information, but endless exploration costs the good options you already have.
power.defence: Decide in advance how many options to explore before committing.

power.title: Decide when the information is ripe
power.principle: Committing before enough information is risky; waiting too long forfeits the best options.
power.defence: Use a benchmark from your first options to judge the rest.

power.title: Know your alternative before you negotiate
power.principle: The strength of your position is the quality of your best option if the deal fails.
power.defence: Never enter a negotiation without knowing your alternative.

power.title: A fair offer is often the strongest offer
power.principle: Offers seen as unfair are often rejected, even when rejection costs the rejecter.
power.defence: Test an offer against what the other side will perceive as fair.

power.title: Trade what each side values least
power.principle: Items valued differently by two people can be traded to create value for both.
power.defence: Ask what each side cares about least, and what it cares about most.

power.title: Expand the pie before dividing it
power.principle: Joint gains are usually larger than any split of a fixed amount.
power.defence: Ask what could make the total larger before arguing about shares.

power.title: Anchor reasonably and concede in steps
power.principle: A reasonable opening and small, shrinking concessions keep a negotiation moving.
power.defence: Make concessions visibly smaller over time, so the other side sees that you are near your limit.

power.title: Hold firm on what matters
power.principle: Concede on details freely, and keep firm on the few points that define your interests.
power.defence: Name your non-negotiables early, so you do not concede them under pressure.

power.title: Do not reward threats
power.principle: Paying for a threat teaches the other side that threats work.
power.defence: Separate a legitimate grievance from a demand made under threat, and address only the grievance.

power.title: Make the right option the best one for them
power.principle: Agreements last when the other side's best option is the one you can live with.
power.defence: Ask what the other side's best alternative is, and whether your offer beats it.

power.title: Price the risk before you bet
power.principle: Decisions under uncertainty should weigh the chance and size of loss, not just the hoped-for gain.
power.defence: Write down the worst plausible outcome and whether you could survive it.

power.title: Guard against being held up
power.principle: Investments that work only with one partner give that partner leverage.
power.defence: Protect specific investments with contracts or shared ownership before making them.

power.title: Avoid single dependence
power.principle: Depending on one supplier, source or person creates a single point of failure.
power.defence: Keep at least one realistic alternative for anything critical.

power.title: Expect responses to incentives
power.principle: People respond to what they are rewarded for, which is not always what you intended.
power.defence: Ask what the incentive rewards, and whether it could be gamed.

power.title: Discipline beats cleverness over time
power.principle: Steady, rule-based play outlasts clever swings in the long run.
power.defence: Set a loss limit and a stopping rule before you start.

power.title: Keep your strategy private
power.principle: Revealing your plan early gives others the chance to prepare.
power.defence: Share what others need to know, and nothing more.

power.title: Control your emotional state
power.principle: Anger and fear are easy to exploit and make predictable mistakes.
power.defence: Pause before any important decision made while angry or afraid.

power.title: Know your own biases
power.principle: The biases that mislead you are the ones others can use against you.
power.defence: List the two biases you are most prone to, and check for them before each big decision.

power.title: Fairness builds durable power
power.principle: Power that rests on fair dealing lasts longer than power that rests on fear.
power.defence: Ask whether your gains would survive being seen by everyone affected.

power.title: Build your own options
power.principle: Having choices is the surest source of power, and the hardest to take away.
power.defence: Invest in skills, relationships and savings that give you exits and alternatives.

defend.signs: A deadline that cannot be checked; pressure not to 'think it over'.
defend.defence: Pause for a set period before deciding. Ask who benefits from the deadline.

defend.signs: 'Only two left', 'this offer ends tonight' with no evidence.
defend.defence: Check the claim independently. Real scarcity survives a short wait.

defend.signs: A favour given unasked, followed by a larger request.
defend.defence: You are not obliged to repay a favour you did not agree to. Say so, kindly.

defend.signs: A small request now, a much larger one next, framed as continuous.
defend.defence: Evaluate each request on its own terms, not as a step in a sequence.

defend.signs: Being cut off from family, friends or independent advice.
defend.defence: Keep outside contacts. Treat pressure to cut them off as a warning sign.

defend.signs: Being told you misremember what was said, repeatedly.
defend.defence: Write down agreements and key conversations. Check them against records.

defend.signs: Each time a condition is met, a new one appears.
defend.defence: Ask for all conditions in writing before you start.

defend.signs: Credentials or titles offered in place of evidence.
defend.defence: Ask for the evidence behind the claim, and check it independently.

defend.signs: Unusual praise followed by an ask you were not expecting.
defend.defence: Notice the sequence. Decide on the request, not the compliment.

defend.signs: Only two options presented, both bad.
defend.defence: Name at least one more option before choosing.

defend.signs: 'You have already put so much in; you cannot stop now.'
defend.defence: Decide on future costs and benefits only.

defend.signs: Separate, different deals offered to each member of a group.
defend.defence: Share terms across the group and compare them openly.

defend.signs: Intense attention and promises early, then coldness when you set a boundary.
defend.defence: Judge consistency over weeks, not intensity over days.

defend.signs: Being made to feel responsible for someone else's difficulty as a lever.
defend.defence: Separate sympathy from obligation. Help on your own terms.

defend.signs: 'Everyone is doing it' with no way to check.
defend.defence: Ask how you would know, and look at what the evidence actually shows.

defend.signs: One party is harsh while another offers relief, to push you toward the second.
defend.defence: Negotiate with the decision-maker, not the messenger, and take time before agreeing.

defend.signs: Only favourable facts are shared, and the rest is withheld.
defend.defence: Ask what is missing, and request the full picture before judging.

research.detail: Write the question as something you could be wrong about, and what evidence would settle it.
Prefer systematic reviews, official statistics, primary documents and peer-reviewed work over summaries and commentary.
Ask how common the outcome is before the evidence arrived. Rare events need strong evidence.
Ask who was studied, how they were chosen, what was compared, and whether results have been replicated.
Ask who pays for the work and who gains if it is believed.
Look for agreement across independent methods and sources, not repetition of one source.
Record sources, dates, confidence and what would change your mind, so you can see later where you were right or wrong.
Set a date to review the conclusion, and update it when new evidence arrives.

research_starting_points: Cialdini, R., Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion (1984): how persuasion works, and how to notice it.
Kahneman, D., Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011): common judgement errors and how to check for them.
Tetlock, P. and Gardner, D., Superforecasting (2015): how calibrated forecasters reason and track their accuracy.
Axelrod, R., The Evolution of Cooperation (1984): how cooperation emerges from repeated interaction.
Ostrom, E., Governing the Commons (1990): how groups manage shared resources without relying only on markets or states.
Schelling, T., The Strategy of Conflict (1960): commitment, bargaining and bargaining under threat.
Machiavelli, N., The Prince (1532, public domain): an early, historically important account of power politics.
Sun Tzu, The Art of War (public domain): a classic on strategy, preparation and deception in conflict.

life.title: Keep a decision journal
life.detail: For important decisions, write the reasoning, the expected outcome, and the date. Review it later to learn what you get right.

life.title: Run a pre-mortem
life.detail: Imagine the plan has failed badly, and list the most likely reasons. Plan against those before you start.

life.title: Sort decisions into reversible and irreversible
life.detail: Decide quickly on reversible choices; take extra care with the ones you cannot undo.

life.title: Protect your alternatives
life.detail: Savings, skills and relationships give you options. Options are what make you hard to pressure.

life.title: Set limits in advance
life.detail: Decide your budget, your time limit and your stopping point before you are under pressure.

life.title: Watch your own biases
life.detail: Notice when you are most sure, most angry, or most tired. Delay big decisions in those states.

life.title: Treat fairness as strategy
life.detail: Relationships and reputations built on fair dealing are the most reliable source of support when times are hard.

life.title: Ask for the full picture
life.detail: Before agreeing to anything important, ask what is missing, what it costs, and who benefits.

life.title: Build friendships through repetition
life.detail: Return to the same recurring setting, such as a class, club or team. Familiarity comes first, then small reciprocal favours, then gradually more openness.

life.title: Make friends by being reliable and curious
life.detail: Keep small promises, follow up on what people tell you, and ask about them. Trust grows from many small kept commitments.

life.title: Build allies around shared interests
life.detail: Name a goal you both want. Make commitments specific and limited, keep contributions visible, and help before you need help. Never create obligations people did not agree to.
